name: Healthcare Realty Trust Incorporated

profile.description: Healthcare Realty Trust is the largest U.S. owner of outpatient medical buildings, leasing properties clustered around leading hospital campuses to health systems and physician groups. The current company was formed by the 2022 merger of Healthcare Realty and Healthcare Trust of America. Under CEO Peter A. Scott (appointed April 2025, formerly Healthpeak CFO), the REIT has cut its dividend, sold non-core assets, formed a joint venture with KKR, and repurchased stock; Q3 2026 normalized FFO was $0.42/share with full-year guidance raised to $1.62-$1.66.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Innovation Track Record (1/3): The 2022 HTA merger doubled the portfolio (FMP revenue rose from $735M in 2020 to $1.18B in 2025) and the KKR strategic joint venture ($211M of acquisitions this quarter, ~$42M at share) is a capital-light model shift, but these are financial restructurings rather than new products [1][3]. AI Deployment (0/2): No AI-enabled products or quantified AI savings; the only technology initiative found is a 2024 commitment to build out a 'data analytics platform' [4]. Market Share Leadership (2/2): Healthcare Realty is the largest owner of outpatient medical buildings in the U.S., with same-store cash NOI growth of 5.1% and 88.0% tenant retention in Q3 2026 [1][7]. Product Pipeline (1/2): Redevelopment and JV acquisition activity is ongoing, but no named development pipeline with dated revenue contribution was disclosed. R&D Intensity (0/1): REITs do not invest in R&D.

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): The company's purpose of owning high-quality outpatient buildings that facilitate the delivery of healthcare is clear and tied to a societal need, but is interchangeable with any healthcare REIT [7]. Community Impact (1/2): The company publishes an annual Corporate Responsibility Report with energy, emissions, and water reduction targets and is rated 'Average' for ESG risk management by Sustainalytics; no distinctive charitable foundation or dollar-quantified community program was found [5][7]. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention data; the business has been through a CEO resignation (November 2024), an interim CEO, and a new CEO from outside (April 2025) plus CFO and GC turnover [4]. Insider Buying (1/2): FMP data show two open-market insider purchases in Q1 2026 and one in Q3 2025 against one sale in each of Q2 and Q3 2026 — roughly balanced, not meaningful net buying [6].

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored as a Dividend stock (weighted 6.07/12). GAAP metrics penalize this REIT for depreciation: ROE of -1.02% and profit margin of -3.95% both score 0, and Yahoo's forward P/E of 462x is meaningless, so a P/FFO proxy of 11.3x ($18.49 / $1.64 normalized FFO guidance midpoint, derived by us) is used and scores 1.0 [1][2]. D/E of 108.5% scores 0.83, revenue fell 3.6% YoY on dispositions (0.55), and the 9.9% 5-year revenue CAGR (FMP, 2020-2025, inflated by the HTA merger) scores 0.99 [2][3]. Dividend: FFO payout of ~58.5% ($0.96/$1.64) scores 0.69; payments every year since the 1993 IPO (33 years) score full 2x weight; but the 2025 cut from $0.31 to $0.24 quarterly leaves 0 years of growth and a negative 5-year dividend CAGR (~-4.4%, $1.20 to $0.96 annual), both 0 [2]. Liquidity floor cleared easily: 4.40M shares x $18.49 = ~$81M daily.

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): Healthcare Realty owns physical outpatient medical buildings on or near hospital campuses, where procedures, imaging, and in-person care cannot be performed by software; no analyst commentary found flags AI as a threat to the business [1][4]. The main indirect risk is that AI-enabled virtual care and remote diagnostics could, over time, reduce demand for some physician office space, which keeps it out of the IMMUNE tier. AI Opportunity (0/1): No AI-related revenue; the company's technology agenda is limited to a data analytics platform for internal decisions [4].

infinite_game.summary: Through Sinek's lens, Healthcare Realty is a well-run real estate vehicle, not a cause-driven organization. The new CEO has made hard, long-term-oriented balance sheet decisions (dividend cut, asset sales, KKR JV, buybacks), but the purpose is functional, leadership churn has been high, and the strategy is about portfolio optimization rather than advancing a vision of better healthcare.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): The stated purpose of providing outpatient buildings that facilitate healthcare delivery describes what the company does, not a future state worth sacrificing for [7]. Strategic communication centers on NOI growth, FFO per share, and leverage targets rather than on improving patient access or care, so the cause does not visibly shape decisions [1].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): The board removed CEO Todd Meredith in November 2024 to take 'a new direction', ran an interim leadership period, then hired an outside CEO in April 2025 while also replacing the CFO and general counsel [4]. That level of top-level turnover in under a year, combined with no evidence of employee retention or empowerment practices, indicates an organization in transition rather than a Circle of Safety.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Management commentary frames competition in terms of capital costs, pricing, and share-price discounts versus healthcare REIT peers rather than learning from rivals' strengths [1]. No evidence of rival-inspired self-improvement language was found.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): The company has meaningfully reshaped itself — the 2022 HTA merger, then under CEO Scott a pivot to a capital-recycling model with large dispositions, a KKR joint venture that moves acquisitions off balance sheet, and 4.2M shares repurchased at $17.74 [1][4]. These are evolutions within outpatient medical real estate, not a reinvention of the business.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Cutting the quarterly dividend 22.6% (from $0.31 to $0.24) in 2025 — an unpopular move for an income REIT — to fund deleveraging and buybacks shows willingness to accept near-term pain for balance sheet durability [2]. The decision was arguably forced by leverage and stock underperformance rather than driven by a cause, so it is one example rather than a pattern.

investment_thesis: Healthcare Realty is a self-help story in a durable asset class. Q3 2026 normalized FFO of $0.42/share, 5.1% same-store cash NOI growth, and a second guidance raise (normalized FFO to $1.62-$1.66, same-store NOI to 4.25%-5.00%) show the operating turnaround under CEO Peter Scott is working [1]. At $18.49 the stock trades at ~11.3x FFO with a 5.2% yield covered at ~58% of FFO, and management is buying back stock (4.2M shares at $17.74) while recycling capital through its KKR joint venture [1][2]. Aging demographics and the shift of care from hospitals to outpatient settings provide a long runway for demand in the largest outpatient medical portfolio in the country.
thesis_continued: The bear case is that the business is shrinking to get better: revenue fell 3.6% YoY and FY2025 revenue of $1.18B was down from $1.34B in 2023 as dispositions outpace growth, and GAAP net losses persist (Q3 2026 EPS of -$0.05) [1][3]. D/E of 108.5% and $4.5B of debt leave the REIT sensitive to refinancing rates, and the 2025 dividend cut broke the income record that dividend investors value [2]. Leadership is still new, and execution on asset sales, JV deployment, and leverage reduction must continue for the P/FFO discount to close.
key_catalysts: Continued FFO guidance beats — normalized FFO guidance already raised to $1.62-$1.66 with same-store cash NOI guidance at 4.25%-5.00%; another raise in Q4 would support multiple expansion from ~11.3x FFO [1]
Share repurchases at a discount to NAV — 4.2M shares bought back at an average $17.74 in Q3 and early October 2026, accretive to FFO per share [1]
KKR joint venture scaling — $211M of acquisitions added this quarter (~$42M at share) lets HR grow fee income and exposure without adding on-balance-sheet leverage [1]
key_risks: Shrinking revenue base — revenue down 3.6% YoY and from $1.34B (2023) to $1.18B (2025) as dispositions continue, which could cap FFO growth if proceeds are not redeployed accretively [2][3]
Leverage and rates — D/E of 108.5% and ~$4.5B of total debt against $29M cash leave FFO exposed to higher refinancing costs [2]
Tenant and occupancy risk — continued tenant troubles or asset sales could pressure cash flows and occupancy, a risk analysts have flagged [4]
